docs.title: GraphReduce
docs.text:
GraphReduce builds model-ready feature tables from relational data. A graph describes which tables are related, how they join, and which entity defines the final row grain. GraphReduce executes the graph from the leaves upward, reducing one-to-many relations before joining them into their parents.

The result is a reproducible alternative to maintaining a large, hand-written chain of joins and aggregations for every ML project.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
New users should follow this path:

  1. Read the fundamentals for the graph model.
  2. Run the quickstart from a repository checkout.
  3. Review time windows before creating a training dataset.
  4. Choose an end-to-end example that matches your backend or modeling goal.

If you already understand the basics, use these direct routes:

Goal Read Define custom dataframe logic Custom node operations Look up graph, node, or edge settings Configuration reference Understand joins and output grain Joins and cardinality Use DuckDB or another SQL backend SQL backends Configure automatic SQL features SQL auto-feature families Reuse a generated SQL plan Frozen SQL plans Compare complete workflows End-to-end examples

docs.title: The graph model
docs.text:
A GraphReduce graph has three parts:

  • A node represents one table or file and owns its data operations.
  • An edge represents a key relationship and its reduction behavior.
  • The parent node defines the intended output grain.

For a customer-to-orders edge, reduce=True means “aggregate orders by their customer foreign key, then join the aggregates to customers.” This avoids the row multiplication that a raw one-to-many join would create.

docs.title: Time semantics
docs.text:
For a cutoff time T, GraphReduce separates feature and label data:

feature rows                       label rows
(T - history, T)                   (T, T + horizon)
───────────────●───────────────────●───────────────
               history start       T

For non-null timestamps the boundaries are strict: rows exactly at T are excluded from both windows. Every time-varying node needs a valid date_key; otherwise GraphReduce cannot apply point-in-time filtering to that node.

See Time windows and leakage safety for the full contract.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pip install graphreduce

Optional integrations are installed as extras:

pip install "graphreduce[duckdb]"
pip install "graphreduce[spark]"
pip install "graphreduce[daft]"
pip install "graphreduce[trino]"
pip install "graphreduce[relbench]"

For development:

git clone https://github.com/wesmadrigal/graphreduce.git
cd graphreduce
pip install -e ".[dev]"

docs.title: Execution paths
docs.text:
Workload Node Execute with Automatic dataframe features DynamicNode GraphReduce.do_transformations() Custom dataframe features GraphReduceNode subclass GraphReduce.do_transformations() SQL-native features SQLNode or backend subclass GraphReduce.do_transformations_sql()

Use a unique prefix for every node regardless of the execution path. Prefixes make joined columns traceable and prevent name collisions.

docs.title: Design goals
docs.text:
GraphReduce emphasizes:

  • explicit relational structure rather than hidden join logic;
  • cardinality-safe aggregation to a declared output grain;
  • consistent historical and future time windows;
  • backend portability where the underlying engines permit it;
  • a gradual path from automatic features to fully custom operations; and
  • inspectable intermediate logic, including generated SQL.

The library is under active development, and support is not perfectly uniform across every compute layer. Validate a representative sample on the backend you intend to use before scaling a production workload.

docs.title: Core Abstractions
docs.text: GraphReduce has a deliberately small object model: tables are nodes, relationships are edges, and one graph coordinates execution.

docs.title: GraphReduce
docs.text:
GraphReduce extends networkx.DiGraph. It stores the table graph and owns configuration that must be consistent across nodes:

  • parent_node: the intended output entity and row grain;
  • compute_layer: the execution backend;
  • cut_date: the point in time at which features are evaluated;
  • compute_period_*: the historical feature window;
  • label_period_*: the future target window;
  • label_node, label_field, and label_operation: optional automatic label configuration; and
  • auto_features: whether GraphReduce should synthesize relation features.

The normal entry points are:

graph.do_transformations()       # dataframe execution
graph.do_transformations_sql()   # SQL execution

For dataframe execution, the final materialized result is graph.parent_node.df.

docs.title: Node types
docs.text:
Every node represents one source relation and requires a unique prefix.

Node Use it when DynamicNode Default loading and automatic dataframe features are sufficient GraphReduceNode subclass A dataframe source needs custom operations SQLNode Operations should be represented as composable SQL Backend SQL subclass The backend needs specialized behavior, such as DuckdbNode or AthenaNode

Common node settings include:

  • fpath: a file path or SQL relation, depending on the node type;
  • fmt: source format such as csv, parquet, or sql;
  • pk: a primary key string or composite-key sequence;
  • prefix: column-lineage prefix, unique within the graph;
  • date_key: the timestamp used for time filtering; and
  • compute_layer: a value from ComputeLayerEnum.

docs.title: DynamicNode
docs.text:
Use DynamicNode for schema-driven dataframe features:

from graphreduce.enum import ComputeLayerEnum
from graphreduce.node import DynamicNode

orders = DynamicNode(
    fpath="orders.parquet",
    fmt="parquet",
    pk="id",
    prefix="ord",
    date_key="created_at",
    compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.pandas,
)

docs.title: Custom GraphReduceNode
docs.text:
A custom subclass owns seven operation hooks. Methods work with self.df; they do not receive a dataframe argument.

import pandas as pd

from graphreduce.node import GraphReduceNode


class OrderNode(GraphReduceNode):
    def do_filters(self):
        self.df = self.df[self.df[self.colabbr("amount")] >= 0]

    def do_annotate(self):
        pass

    def do_normalize(self):
        pass

    def do_reduce(self, reduce_key):
        key = self.colabbr(reduce_key)
        return self.prep_for_features().groupby(key).agg(
            **{
                self.colabbr("amount_sum"): pd.NamedAgg(
                    column=self.colabbr("amount"), aggfunc="sum"
                )
            }
        )

    def do_labels(self, reduce_key):
        pass

    def do_post_join_annotate(self):
        pass

    def do_post_join_filters(self):
        pass

The key helpers are:

  • colabbr("amount") returns the prefixed physical column name;
  • prep_for_features() applies the node's historical window; and
  • prep_for_labels() applies the node's future label window.

docs.title: SQLNode
docs.text:
SQL methods return sqlop objects rather than mutating self.df. GraphReduce compiles those operations and manages intermediate backend references.

from graphreduce.enum import ComputeLayerEnum, SQLOpType
from graphreduce.models import sqlop
from graphreduce.node import SQLNode


class OrderSQLNode(SQLNode):
    def do_reduce(self, reduce_key):
        key = self.colabbr(reduce_key)
        return [
            sqlop(
                optype=SQLOpType.aggfunc,
                opval=f"sum({self.colabbr('amount')}) as {self.colabbr('amount_sum')}",
            ),
            sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.agg, opval=key),
        ]

See SQL backends and dynamic queries for complete examples.

docs.title: Edges
docs.text:
An entity edge records the direction, join keys, and reduction behavior:

graph.add_entity_edge(
    parent_node=customers,
    relation_node=orders,
    parent_key="id",
    relation_key="customer_id",
    reduce=True,
)

The direction is meaningful: the relation is processed and joined into its parent. With reduce=True, GraphReduce aggregates the relation to its foreign key before the join.

Both keys may be ordered tuples for composite relationships. Their lengths must match.

docs.title: Prefixes and physical columns
docs.text:
Nodes prefix columns as data enters the graph. An orders.amount source column on a node with prefix="ord" becomes ord_amount. Always use colabbr() in custom operations instead of hard-coding the transformed name.

Prefixes must be unique across all graph nodes. They provide lineage and avoid ambiguous columns after repeated joins.

docs.title: Put configuration at the right level
docs.text:
• Put table-specific behavior and schema meaning on the node.
  • Put relationship cardinality and join keys on the edge.
  • Put shared execution, time-window, label, and graph-wide automatic-feature settings on GraphReduce.

This separation is the core design constraint behind the library.

docs.title: Configuration Reference
docs.text: This page covers the settings needed for most graphs. The Python signatures remain the source of truth for less common backend-specific and experimental options.

docs.title: Graph identity and execution
docs.text: Parameter Meaning name Human-readable graph name parent_node Node that anchors traversal and normally defines output grain compute_layer Backend selected from ComputeLayerEnum auto_features Generate schema-aware relation features during reduction debug Enable additional diagnostic logging train Include training-only behavior such as label computation; scoring graphs normally set this to False

docs.title: Time windows
docs.text:
Parameter Meaning cut_date Point-in-time reference for feature and label windows compute_period_val Size of the historical feature window compute_period_unit Unit for the feature-window value label_period_val Size of the future label window label_period_unit Unit for the label-window value

If label_node is set, both label-period settings are required. See Time windows and leakage safety for exact boundaries.

docs.title: Labels
docs.text:
Parameter Meaning label_node Relation from which the target is computed label_field Source field passed to automatic label aggregation label_operation Aggregation string or callable, such as count, sum, or bool

For DynamicNode, GraphReduce calls the default label implementation. A custom GraphReduceNode supplies do_labels(reduce_key) instead.

Automatic labels are left-joined to the parent. An entity with no matching label-window row therefore receives null, not an implicit zero.

docs.title: Traversal
docs.text:
Parameter Meaning auto_feature_hops_back Depth limit for descendant traversal from the parent auto_feature_hops_front Limit for optional joins through predecessor nodes

Keep auto_feature_hops_back at least as deep as the child relations that must contribute to the output. The default is 2.

docs.title: SQL execution
docs.text:
Parameter Meaning sql_client Backend client shared with SQL nodes lazy_execution Defer backend execution where supported dry_run Compile/log SQL without executing it checkpoint_schema Schema used for SQL intermediate materialization

Automatic SQL feature settings are documented separately under SQL auto-feature families.

docs.title: Source and schema
docs.text:
Parameter Meaning fpath File path or SQL relation, depending on node type fmt Storage/source format such as csv, parquet, or sql pk Primary key as a string or ordered composite-key sequence prefix Required column-lineage prefix; must be unique in the graph date_key Timestamp used by feature and label filtering columns Known source columns, especially useful for SQL nodes compute_layer Node backend; normally matches the graph backend

Graph hydration overwrites shared execution and time settings on nodes with the graph-level values. Put one cutoff and one window policy on the graph unless a specialized workflow explicitly requires something else.

docs.title: SQL-only additions
docs.text: SQLNode accepts a backend client, optional table_name, and optional lists of sqlop values for each operation hook. A backend subclass may require more connection, catalog, or storage configuration.

docs.title: Entity edges
docs.text:
GraphReduce.add_entity_edge() accepts:

Parameter Meaning parent_node Destination of the relation's features relation_node Child relation being joined upward parent_key Key on the parent relation_key Matching key on the relation relation_type Relationship label; normally parent_child reduce Aggregate the relation before joining reduce_after_join Join first and reduce the enriched parent afterward

parent_key and relation_key must have the same number of columns. reduce and reduce_after_join cannot both be true.

docs.title: Results and inspection
docs.text:
Path Result graph.parent_node.df Materialized dataframe result graph.sql_ops Generated SQL statements in execution order graph.get_executed_op_records() Structured SQL operation records graph.freeze_execution_plan() Serializable record of a completed SQL plan graph.plot_graph(path) Interactive HTML visualization of graph topology

For SQL plan reuse, see Frozen SQL plans.

docs.title: Feature Schema Profiles
docs.text: A feature schema profile records which columns are structural, predictive, or unsafe. Fit it on training data before automatic feature generation so schema decisions do not learn from validation or test distributions.

docs.title: Create a manifest
docs.text:
from graphreduce.feature_schema import profile_feature_schema

manifest = profile_feature_schema(
    training_sample,
    primary_keys="study_id",
    foreign_keys=("sponsor_id",),
    date_keys="event_time",
    target_columns="outcome",
    unsafe_columns=("future_duration",),
    source="studies",
)

The manifest separates:

  • primary and foreign keys used for graph structure;
  • date keys used for temporal behavior;
  • target columns used for supervision;
  • unsafe columns that must not become features; and
  • eligible model features with inferred types.

Typical consumers are:

node.columns = list(manifest.graph_columns)
categorical_columns = manifest.categorical_columns

docs.title: Infer through a node
docs.text:
Nodes expose the same workflow:

manifest = node.infer_feature_manifest(
    training_sample,
    foreign_keys=("sponsor_id",),
    target_columns="outcome",
    unsafe_columns=("future_duration",),
    apply_columns=True,
)

With apply_columns=True, the inferred graph columns are assigned back to the node.

docs.title: Prevent schema leakage
docs.text:
Use only the training sample to decide:

  • semantic and physical types;
  • missing-value coverage;
  • categorical cardinality;
  • feature inclusion; and
  • any value-frequency threshold.

Validation and test frames may be aligned to the completed manifest, but must not change it.

GraphReduce cannot determine availability time from a dtype or column name. A field such as resolved_at, final_status, or lifetime_value may contain future information even when it looks harmless. Put mutable, post-outcome, or future-derived fields in unsafe_columns based on dataset knowledge.

docs.title: Relationship to automatic features
docs.text:
The manifest decides which columns are safe and how they should be understood. Automatic feature families decide which relational operations to generate from those columns. For example, a safe categorical event_type can produce bounded indicators, while a safe numeric amount can produce reductions or windowed summaries.

See SQL auto-feature families for those generation controls.

docs.title: SQL Auto-Feature Families
docs.text:
GraphReduce can generate relational features while compiling a graph through GraphReduce.do_transformations_sql(). A feature family is a bounded group of SQL expressions created when a child relation is reduced to its parent key.

Only base is enabled by default. Every other family is opt-in.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text: Family Question it answers Main requirement base How much activity occurred, and what are its basic summaries? None temporal How did numeric values differ across lookback windows? date_key and ts_periods state What were the latest values and the last N events? date_key sequence Was activity steady, recent, or bursty? date_key and ts_periods conditional What kinds of activity occurred? Eligible categories or predicate annotations episode How many rows and distinct events occurred? A primary key for distinct-event counts semantic Which domain concepts should become features? annotation_expressions or auto-annotation context How did a value compare with its peers? Explicit context_keys

docs.title: Configure a node
docs.text:
Feature families can be selected on an individual SQL node:

from graphreduce.enum import ComputeLayerEnum
from graphreduce.node import DuckdbNode

events = DuckdbNode(
    fpath="events",
    fmt="sql",
    pk="event_id",
    prefix="evt",
    date_key="event_time",
    compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.duckdb,
    feature_families=("base", "temporal", "state", "sequence", "conditional"),
    ts_periods=(7, 30, 90, 365),
    state_lags=(1, 2, 3, 5),
    state_windows=(3, 5, 10),
    feature_family_max_columns=4,
    categorical_cardinality_threshold=20,
    categorical_top_k=5,
)

Or set schema-independent defaults on the graph:

graph = GraphReduce(
    parent_node=customers,
    compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.duckdb,
    auto_features=True,
    feature_families=("base", "temporal", "sequence"),
    ts_periods=(7, 30, 90, 365),
    feature_family_max_columns=4,
    categorical_cardinality_threshold=20,
    categorical_top_k=5,
)

graph.do_transformations_sql()

Graph-level feature settings default to None. When omitted, the node's value is preserved; when supplied, the graph value overrides every node during graph hydration. Node-specific concepts such as annotation_expressions and context_keys should remain on the node whose schema defines them.

docs.title: Time windows
docs.text:
ts_periods contains lookback lengths in days. Each period is evaluated relative to the current point-in-time reference when one is available, or to the graph's cut_date otherwise.

Three controls work together:

  • date_key identifies the event timestamp on the node.
  • compute_period_val and compute_period_unit bound all available history.
  • ts_periods creates summaries within that already-bounded history.

A 365-day ts_periods entry cannot recover rows if the graph's compute window contains only 90 days. Set ts_periods=() to disable rolling-window features.

docs.title: base: schema-aware summaries
docs.text:
The base family inspects a sample and emits aggregations appropriate for the inferred physical and semantic types:

  • identifier-like columns contribute a count without duplicating the same count for every identifier;
  • numeric columns use compatible functions from type_func_map;
  • booleans produce true counts and shares;
  • dates and timestamps produce configured date summaries;
  • eligible categorical columns produce distinct counts and bounded count/share/presence features; and
  • text-like columns can produce inexpensive length, word-count, empty-value, URL, number, and punctuation summaries.

For a time-series relation, base also creates recency, windowed event counts, and adjacent-window change ratios.

A categorical column is eligible only when its observed cardinality is at most categorical_cardinality_threshold. At most categorical_top_k frequent values are expanded; an other bucket is added when the top-value limit omits eligible values. Higher-cardinality columns are skipped.

Text summaries are controlled independently by auto_text_features. They do not tokenize, embed, or call a language model.

docs.title: Bounded numeric distributions in base
docs.text:
SQL base now also emits numeric empirical-CDF summaries automatically. This does not add another family or another graph-search dimension. For each selected numeric payload it adds finite-value coverage and up to seven fractions of observed rows at or below frozen historical quantile thresholds. Unlike a mean, these summaries retain where mass lies within the value range.

  • At most min(feature_family_max_columns, 16) source columns are considered, in the existing source/annotation order. Constant, binary, unobserved and identifier-like inputs, declared keys/dates/context keys, and already reduced features are skipped. This prevents CDF-of-CDF or CDF-of-aggregate expansion.
  • At most eight columns are added per eligible input: 128 per reduction at the hard ceiling, or 32 with a four-column budget. Existing base operations take priority within feature_family_max_features_per_column; the CDF extension uses only the remaining allowance. Ordinary propagation of these fractions still follows feature_propagation_max_functions_per_column.
  • Calibration reads at most 20,000 historical rows and the selected numeric columns, using the same cutoff and lookback predicates as reduction, before LIMIT, including per-example date-node boundaries. Key/date/value ordering makes this sample deterministic. It is bounded, not an exact whole-table quantile computation. It uses observed-value (lower) quantiles at eighths.
  • Thresholds are embedded as numeric SQL literals. Freeze the training graph with freeze_execution_plan() and apply that plan to validation/prediction; replay does not recalibrate thresholds or add columns to an old plan.
  • NaN, infinities and NULL do not enter CDF denominators. All-missing groups have zero finite coverage and NULL CDFs. Missing child groups remain NULL after the parent join.

Feature names end in __cdf_coverage_avg and __cdf_q0_avg, etc. Their avg suffix preserves bounded aggregation through deeper paths; an average of child CDFs is a summary of child summaries, not an exact pooled leaf distribution.

For a compatibility ablation, set base_distribution_features=False on the node or graph. The default is True on SQL nodes; graph-level None preserves node settings. Direct low-level sql_auto_features(sample, ...) callers must provide a historical training sample, optionally through distribution_sample. Normal auto_features/graph execution performs the historical SQL calibration. This extension does not yet change the Pandas/Spark/Daft auto-aggregation paths or automatically create semantic text embeddings or parent-only annotations.

docs.title: temporal: windowed numeric values
docs.text:
For each selected numeric column and lookback period, temporal generates windowed sum, avg, min, and max features. The reduce key, date column, and identifier-like values are excluded.

Approximate feature count for N selected numeric columns and P periods:

4 × N × P

Use feature_family_max_columns to keep this family bounded on wide tables.

docs.title: sequence: activity shape
docs.text:
sequence describes cadence without exposing an ordered event list. It can generate:

  • events per day within each period;
  • each period's share of lifetime activity;
  • burst ratios between adjacent periods;
  • the lifetime active span; and
  • lifetime activity per active day.

These features help distinguish steady activity, recent bursts, and dormant entities with similar lifetime counts.

docs.title: state: ordered event state
docs.text:
state ranks each entity's rows after point-in-time filtering and before reduction. For selected numeric values it emits the latest value, configured lags, latest change, and mean/min/max/count/variance/trend summaries over configured trailing row counts. For categorical and relationship identifiers it preserves the latest and previous values, a change flag, and recent diversity.

Unlike day-based temporal windows, state_windows counts observations. The last five races, purchases, visits, or treatments therefore remain available across irregular event cadences and long inactive periods. state_lags and state_windows default to (1, 2, 3, 5) and (3, 5, 10) respectively.

The rank is computed inside a filtered derived table, so rows on or after a strict cutoff cannot become latest-state features.

docs.title: conditional: activity composition
docs.text:
conditional selects conditions from two sources:

  • predicate columns created by semantic annotation; and
  • frequent values from categorical columns within the cardinality threshold.

For each selected condition and period, it generates count, share, and presence features, plus count-change ratios between adjacent periods. Semantic predicates are selected before generic categories.

This family can grow quickly. Bound both feature_family_max_columns and categorical_top_k.

docs.title: episode: rows versus distinct events
docs.text:
episode emits a total row count and, when a primary key is available, a distinct primary-key count. Time-series nodes also receive those counts by lookback period.

This distinction is useful after many-to-many joins: the row count measures join volume, while the distinct count better approximates underlying events.

docs.title: semantic: explicit domain meaning
docs.text:
semantic compiles caller-supplied SQL expressions before reduction:

events = DuckdbNode(
    # ...normal node configuration...
    feature_families=("base", "semantic", "conditional", "temporal"),
    annotation_expressions={
        "is_verified": "{status} = 'verified'",
        "is_high_value": "{amount} >= 100",
        "line_value": ("value", "{amount} * {quantity}"),
    },
)

A plain expression is treated as a predicate and becomes a 0/1 indicator. The ("value", expression) form preserves a numeric result for normal aggregation. Braced placeholders are resolved against the node's columns.

The family does not guess business meaning from names. With auto_annotate_features=True, it can additionally infer a bounded set of categorical indicators, text indicators, and category-gated numeric values.

docs.title: context: peer-relative values
docs.text:
context compares numeric values within an explicit peer group before the child is reduced:

items = DuckdbNode(
    # ...normal node configuration...
    feature_families=("base", "context"),
    context_keys=("category_id",),
)

For each context key, GraphReduce can create peer-group size and the difference between a row's numeric value and its peer-group average. The resulting values are then aggregated to the parent.

GraphReduce deliberately does not infer peer groups. A plausible but incorrect group creates misleading features, so context_keys is required.

docs.title: Keep the feature budget deliberate
docs.text:
The most important controls are:

Setting Controls feature_families Families enabled on a node ts_periods Count and duration of time windows state_lags Ordered event positions retained by state state_windows Trailing row counts summarized by state feature_family_max_columns Source columns or conditions used by expanding families feature_family_max_features_per_column Derived features emitted per selected column categorical_cardinality_threshold Maximum observed cardinality for automatic categories categorical_top_k Values expanded per eligible category auto_text_features Automatic text summaries annotation_expressions Deterministic domain predicates and values context_keys Explicit peer groups

A practical rollout is:

  1. Establish a baseline with ("base",).
  2. Add temporal for meaningful numeric measurements.
  3. Add state when the latest event or last-N observations describe current state.
  4. Add sequence when cadence or burstiness may matter.
  5. Add conditional for important statuses or categories.
  6. Add episode when rows and logical events differ.
  7. Add semantic for known domain concepts.
  8. Add context only when the peer group is unambiguous.

Feature counts multiply across columns, periods, relations, and graph hops. Enable a family where its signal is plausible instead of applying a maximal configuration to every node.

docs.title: Automated Feature Engineering
docs.text:
This guide builds a multi-table customer feature frame with GraphReduce.do_transformations() and auto_features=True. Run the examples from the repository root; they use the CSV files in tests/data/cust_data/.

It covers:

  1. Building a graph of related tabular entities.
  2. Enforcing point-in-time windows with cut_date + compute period.
  3. Automatically generating aggregate features on child tables.
  4. Generating a label and joining everything back to a parent grain.

docs.title: Dataframe example
docs.text:
import datetime
from graphreduce.node import DynamicNode
from graphreduce.graph_reduce import GraphReduce
from graphreduce.enum import ComputeLayerEnum, PeriodUnit

base = "tests/data/cust_data"

# Each node gets a unique prefix so merged columns keep table lineage.
nodes = {
    "cust": DynamicNode(
        fpath=f"{base}/cust.csv",
        fmt="csv",
        pk="id",
        prefix="cu",
        date_key=None,
        compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.pandas,
    ),
    "orders": DynamicNode(
        fpath=f"{base}/orders.csv",
        fmt="csv",
        pk="id",
        prefix="ord",
        date_key="ts",
        compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.pandas,
    ),
    "order_products": DynamicNode(
        fpath=f"{base}/order_products.csv",
        fmt="csv",
        pk="id",
        prefix="op",
        date_key=None,
        compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.pandas,
    ),
    "notifications": DynamicNode(
        fpath=f"{base}/notifications.csv",
        fmt="csv",
        pk="id",
        prefix="notif",
        date_key="ts",
        compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.pandas,
    ),
    "notification_interactions": DynamicNode(
        fpath=f"{base}/notification_interactions.csv",
        fmt="csv",
        pk="id",
        prefix="ni",
        date_key="ts",
        compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.pandas,
    ),
}

gr = GraphReduce(
    name="customers_auto_fe",
    parent_node=nodes["cust"],
    fmt="csv",
    compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.pandas,
    cut_date=datetime.datetime(2023, 9, 1),
    compute_period_val=365,
    compute_period_unit=PeriodUnit.day,
    auto_features=True,
    auto_feature_hops_front=1,
    auto_feature_hops_back=2,
    label_node=nodes["orders"],
    label_operation="count",
    label_field="id",
    label_period_val=60,
    label_period_unit=PeriodUnit.day,
)

for node in nodes.values():
    gr.add_node(node)

# Graph topology:
# cust -> orders -> order_products
# cust -> notifications -> notification_interactions
gr.add_entity_edge(
    parent_node=nodes["cust"],
    relation_node=nodes["orders"],
    parent_key="id",
    relation_key="customer_id",
    reduce=True,
)
gr.add_entity_edge(
    parent_node=nodes["orders"],
    relation_node=nodes["order_products"],
    parent_key="id",
    relation_key="order_id",
    reduce=True,
)
gr.add_entity_edge(
    parent_node=nodes["cust"],
    relation_node=nodes["notifications"],
    parent_key="id",
    relation_key="customer_id",
    reduce=True,
)
gr.add_entity_edge(
    parent_node=nodes["notifications"],
    relation_node=nodes["notification_interactions"],
    parent_key="id",
    relation_key="notification_id",
    reduce=True,
)

gr.do_transformations()

# Final training / analytics frame at customer grain.
df = gr.parent_node.df
print(df.shape)
print(df.head())

assert df["cu_id"].is_unique
assert "ord_id_label" in df.columns

The graph is evaluated from its leaves upward. order_products is reduced to order grain before the enriched order table is reduced to customer grain; notification_interactions follows the same path through notifications.

The bundled data contains only four customers and is intended to demonstrate materialization, not meaningful model evaluation. Use the XGBoost or TabPFN example for the modeling step.

docs.title: SQL example with do_transformations_sql()
docs.text:
import datetime
import sqlite3
import pandas as pd
from graphreduce.graph_reduce import GraphReduce
from graphreduce.node import SQLNode
from graphreduce.models import sqlop
from graphreduce.enum import ComputeLayerEnum, PeriodUnit, SQLOpType

base = "tests/data/cust_data"
conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")

# Load csv files into sqlite tables for this example.
pd.read_csv(f"{base}/cust.csv").to_sql("cust", conn, index=False, if_exists="replace")
pd.read_csv(f"{base}/orders.csv").to_sql("orders", conn, index=False, if_exists="replace")
pd.read_csv(f"{base}/order_products.csv").to_sql("order_products", conn, index=False, if_exists="replace")


class OrdersSQLNode(SQLNode):
    def do_reduce(self, reduce_key):
        return [
            sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.aggfunc, opval=f"count(*) as {self.colabbr('id_count')}"),
            sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.aggfunc, opval=f"min({self.colabbr('ts')}) as {self.colabbr('ts_min')}"),
            sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.aggfunc, opval=f"max({self.colabbr('ts')}) as {self.colabbr('ts_max')}"),
            sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.agg, opval=f"{self.colabbr(reduce_key)}"),
        ]

    def do_labels(self, reduce_key):
        return [
            sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.aggfunc, opval=f"count(*) as {self.colabbr('id_label')}"),
            sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.agg, opval=f"{self.colabbr(reduce_key)}"),
        ]


class OrderProductsSQLNode(SQLNode):
    def do_reduce(self, reduce_key):
        return [
            sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.aggfunc, opval=f"count(*) as {self.colabbr('id_count')}"),
            sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.aggfunc, opval=f"count(distinct {self.colabbr('product_id')}) as {self.colabbr('product_id_nunique')}"),
            sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.agg, opval=f"{self.colabbr(reduce_key)}"),
        ]


cust = SQLNode(
    fpath="cust",
    prefix="cu",
    client=conn,
    columns=["id", "name"],
    compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.sqlite,
    date_key=None,
)
orders = OrdersSQLNode(
    fpath="orders",
    prefix="ord",
    client=conn,
    columns=["id", "customer_id", "ts"],
    compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.sqlite,
    date_key="ts",
)
order_products = OrderProductsSQLNode(
    fpath="order_products",
    prefix="op",
    client=conn,
    columns=["id", "order_id", "product_id"],
    compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.sqlite,
    date_key=None,
)

gr = GraphReduce(
    name="customers_auto_fe_sql",
    parent_node=cust,
    compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.sqlite,
    sql_client=conn,
    cut_date=datetime.datetime(2023, 9, 1),
    compute_period_val=365,
    compute_period_unit=PeriodUnit.day,
    label_node=orders,
    label_period_val=60,
    label_period_unit=PeriodUnit.day,
    # Optional: collect SQL without executing statements.
    # dry_run=True,
)

for node in [cust, orders, order_products]:
    gr.add_node(node)

gr.add_entity_edge(
    parent_node=cust,
    relation_node=orders,
    parent_key="id",
    relation_key="customer_id",
    reduce=True,
)
gr.add_entity_edge(
    parent_node=orders,
    relation_node=order_products,
    parent_key="id",
    relation_key="order_id",
    reduce=True,
)

# SQL pipeline entrypoint.
gr.do_transformations_sql()

# Generated SQL operations (in execution order).
for stmt in gr.sql_ops:
    if isinstance(stmt, str):
        print(stmt)

# Materialized output at customer grain.
out = cust.get_sample()
print(out.columns)
print(out.head())

docs.title: What to expect
docs.text:
After execution, gr.parent_node.df is a customer-grain dataset that includes:

  • base customer columns (cu_*)
  • reduced and auto-generated features propagated upward from child tables (ord_*, op_*, notif_*, ni_*)
  • label columns for supervised learning (for example ord_id_label)

This is the typical batch ML/AI output shape: one row per parent entity with historical multi-table features and optional future-looking labels.

docs.title: Define Custom Node Operations
docs.text: Use a GraphReduceNode subclass when automatic features are not sufficient. The node becomes the single home for logic specific to one source table.

docs.title: Required methods
docs.text:
Custom nodes implement seven hooks:

from graphreduce.node import GraphReduceNode


class MyNode(GraphReduceNode):
    def do_filters(self):
        pass

    def do_annotate(self):
        pass

    def do_normalize(self):
        pass

    def do_reduce(self, reduce_key):
        pass

    def do_labels(self, reduce_key):
        pass

    def do_post_join_annotate(self):
        pass

    def do_post_join_filters(self):
        pass

Methods use self.df; they do not receive a dataframe argument. Leave an unused hook as pass.

docs.title: A complete order node
docs.text:
import pandas as pd

from graphreduce.node import GraphReduceNode


class OrderNode(GraphReduceNode):
    def do_filters(self):
        amount = self.colabbr("amount")
        self.df = self.df[self.df[amount].between(0, 100_000)]

    def do_annotate(self):
        amount = self.colabbr("amount")
        self.df[self.colabbr("is_large")] = self.df[amount] >= 1_000

    def do_normalize(self):
        pass

    def do_reduce(self, reduce_key):
        key = self.colabbr(reduce_key)
        history = self.prep_for_features()
        return history.groupby(key).agg(
            **{
                self.colabbr("order_count"): pd.NamedAgg(
                    column=self.colabbr("id"), aggfunc="count"
                ),
                self.colabbr("amount_sum"): pd.NamedAgg(
                    column=self.colabbr("amount"), aggfunc="sum"
                ),
                self.colabbr("amount_max"): pd.NamedAgg(
                    column=self.colabbr("amount"), aggfunc="max"
                ),
                self.colabbr("large_order_count"): pd.NamedAgg(
                    column=self.colabbr("is_large"), aggfunc="sum"
                ),
            }
        )

    def do_labels(self, reduce_key):
        key = self.colabbr(reduce_key)
        future = self.prep_for_labels()
        labels = future.groupby(key).agg(
            **{
                self.colabbr("order_label"): pd.NamedAgg(
                    column=self.colabbr("id"), aggfunc="count"
                )
            }
        )
        return labels

    def do_post_join_annotate(self):
        pass

    def do_post_join_filters(self):
        pass

Instantiate it like any other node:

from graphreduce.enum import ComputeLayerEnum

orders = OrderNode(
    fpath="orders.csv",
    fmt="csv",
    pk="id",
    prefix="ord",
    date_key="ts",
    compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.pandas,
)

When the graph is hydrated, its shared cutoff and time periods are pushed to the node.

docs.title: Two helpers prevent common mistakes
docs.text:
self.colabbr(name) returns the physical prefixed column. For example, self.colabbr("amount") returns ord_amount when the prefix is ord.

self.prep_for_features() and self.prep_for_labels() return the appropriate time slices. Call them inside reduction and label logic instead of grouping the unfiltered dataframe.

docs.title: Reduction contract
docs.text:
do_reduce(reduce_key) must return data keyed by the prefixed relation key. On an edge from customers to orders, GraphReduce calls orders.do_reduce("customer_id") and expects one aggregate row per ord_customer_id.

If you return duplicate relation keys, the later join can multiply parent rows. Add a focused assertion while developing a node:

reduced = orders.do_reduce("customer_id")
assert reduced.index.is_unique

docs.title: Post-join logic
docs.text: Use do_post_join_annotate or do_post_join_filters only for expressions that need columns from a child already joined into the node. When execution order depends on particular children, declare a post-join dependency.

docs.title: Freezing and Replaying SQL Execution Plans
docs.text:
This page shows how to:

  1. run a SQL-backed GraphReduce graph with train=True and auto_features=True
  2. freeze the exact executed sqlop instances
  3. replay those same ops into a fresh train=True graph
  4. replay those same ops into a fresh train=False graph

The important point is that GraphReduce.freeze_execution_plan() freezes the executed SQL operation program, not just the final dataframe. That means a later graph can reuse the same per-method sqlop instances instead of dynamically recomputing feature SQL.

docs.title: What Gets Frozen
docs.text:
After do_transformations_sql() runs, GraphReduce stores structured execution records for methods such as:

  • do_data
  • do_annotate
  • do_filters
  • do_normalize
  • do_reduce
  • do_labels
  • do_post_join_annotate
  • do_post_join_filters

freeze_execution_plan() returns those executed ops grouped by method and also preserves the execution order by node and edge. apply_execution_plan(plan) loads that frozen plan into a fresh graph so do_transformations_sql() can replay the same method outputs.

When replaying into train=False:

  • label ops are not applied
  • label-dependent post-join ops are not applied
  • date-node joins are not attempted
  • date literals in frozen SQL ops are rebound to the receiving graph's current cut_date

If you do not pass cut_date to the scoring graph, that graph keeps its normal default behavior, which is datetime.datetime.now().

docs.title: Simple Dataset
docs.text:
This example uses the same sqlite dataset across all three runs:

  • cust
  • orders
  • notifications

The customer node also has a post-join annotation that depends on the label column created from the orders node during training.

import datetime
import sqlite3
import pandas as pd

from graphreduce.graph_reduce import GraphReduce
from graphreduce.node import SQLNode
from graphreduce.enum import ComputeLayerEnum, PeriodUnit, SQLOpType
from graphreduce.models import sqlop

def setup_sqlite():
    conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")

    pd.DataFrame(
        [
            {"id": 1, "name": "alex"},
            {"id": 2, "name": "blair"},
            {"id": 3, "name": "casey"},
            {"id": 4, "name": "devon"},
        ]
    ).to_sql("cust", conn, index=False, if_exists="replace")

    pd.DataFrame(
        [
            {"id": 1, "customer_id": 1, "ts": "2023-01-05", "amount": 10.0},
            {"id": 2, "customer_id": 1, "ts": "2023-06-01", "amount": 25.0},
            {"id": 3, "customer_id": 2, "ts": "2023-04-15", "amount": 5.0},
            {"id": 4, "customer_id": 4, "ts": "2023-05-20", "amount": 99.0},
        ]
    ).to_sql("orders", conn, index=False, if_exists="replace")

    pd.DataFrame(
        [
            {"id": 1, "customer_id": 1, "ts": "2023-06-10"},
            {"id": 2, "customer_id": 1, "ts": "2023-06-11"},
            {"id": 3, "customer_id": 3, "ts": "2023-03-01"},
        ]
    ).to_sql("notifications", conn, index=False, if_exists="replace")

    return conn

def build_graph(conn, train, cut_date=None):
    orders = SQLNode(
        fpath="orders",
        pk="id",
        prefix="ord",
        client=conn,
        compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.sqlite,
        columns=["id", "customer_id", "ts", "amount"],
        date_key="ts",
    )

    cust = SQLNode(
        fpath="cust",
        pk="id",
        prefix="cust",
        client=conn,
        compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.sqlite,
        columns=["id", "name"],
        do_post_join_annotate_ops=[
            sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.select, opval="*"),
            sqlop(
                optype=SQLOpType.select,
                opval="case when ord_id_label > 0 then 1 else 0 end as has_order_label",
            ),
        ] if train else None,
        do_post_join_annotate_requires=[orders],
    )

    notifications = SQLNode(
        fpath="notifications",
        pk="id",
        prefix="not",
        client=conn,
        compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.sqlite,
        columns=["id", "customer_id", "ts"],
        date_key="ts",
    )

    kwargs = dict(
        name=f"cust_sql_plan_train_{train}",
        parent_node=cust,
        compute_period_unit=PeriodUnit.day,
        compute_period_val=730,
        label_node=orders,
        label_field="id",
        label_operation="bool",
        label_period_unit=PeriodUnit.day,
        label_period_val=90,
        compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.sqlite,
        use_temp_tables=True,
        lazy_execution=False,
        auto_features=True,
        auto_feature_hops_back=3,
        auto_feature_hops_front=0,
        sql_client=conn,
        date_filters_on_agg=True,
        train=train,
    )
    if cut_date is not None:
        kwargs["cut_date"] = cut_date

    gr = GraphReduce(**kwargs)
    gr.add_node(cust)
    gr.add_node(orders)
    gr.add_node(notifications)
    gr.add_entity_edge(cust, notifications, parent_key="id", relation_key="customer_id", reduce=True)
    gr.add_entity_edge(cust, orders, parent_key="id", relation_key="customer_id", reduce=True)
    return gr

docs.title: Example 1: train=True with Dynamic Auto-Generated Features
docs.text:
This is the normal training path. GraphReduce inspects the graph, auto-generates SQL feature ops where needed, executes labels, and records the executed SQL ops.

train_cut_date = datetime.datetime(2023, 6, 30)

train_conn = setup_sqlite()
train_gr = build_graph(train_conn, train=True, cut_date=train_cut_date)
train_gr.do_transformations_sql()

train_df = pd.read_sql_query(
    f"select * from {train_gr.parent_node._cur_data_ref}",
    train_conn,
).sort_values("cust_id")

frozen_plan = train_gr.freeze_execution_plan()
sql_ops_by_method = train_gr.get_executed_sqlops_by_method(exclude_date_filters=True)

print(sorted(sql_ops_by_method))
print(train_df.columns.tolist())

What happened in this run:

  • do_reduce may include auto-generated SQL ops from sql_auto_features
  • do_labels executes because this is a training graph
  • do_post_join_annotate executes after the label join because it depends on ord_id_label
  • freeze_execution_plan() captures the exact executed sqlop sequences

docs.title: Example 2: train=True Replaying a Previously Frozen Plan
docs.text:
Now create a brand-new graph against the same dataset and same training cut date. Instead of dynamically generating features again, load the frozen plan first.

replay_train_conn = setup_sqlite()
replay_train_gr = build_graph(replay_train_conn, train=True, cut_date=train_cut_date)

replay_train_gr.apply_execution_plan(frozen_plan)
replay_train_gr.do_transformations_sql()

replay_train_df = pd.read_sql_query(
    f"select * from {replay_train_gr.parent_node._cur_data_ref}",
    replay_train_conn,
).sort_values("cust_id")

replay_train_sql_ops = replay_train_gr.get_executed_sqlops_by_method(
    exclude_date_filters=True
)

print("do_labels" in replay_train_sql_ops)
print(train_df.equals(replay_train_df))

What changed in this run:

  • the graph shape is the same
  • the executed SQL ops are loaded from frozen_plan
  • do_transformations_sql() replays the frozen sqlop outputs by node, method, and edge
  • do_labels still executes because this graph is still train=True
  • the output should match the original training run

This is useful when you want reproducible SQL feature generation across repeated training jobs.

docs.title: Example 3: train=False Replaying Frozen Features on the Same Dataset
docs.text:
Now build the same graph again, but this time for scoring.

Do not pass a scoring cut_date here if you want the graph to keep its normal train=False behavior. In that case the graph uses its current default cut_date, which is datetime.datetime.now().

score_conn = setup_sqlite()
score_gr = build_graph(score_conn, train=False)

score_gr.apply_execution_plan(frozen_plan)
score_gr.do_transformations_sql()

score_df = pd.read_sql_query(
    f"select * from {score_gr.parent_node._cur_data_ref}",
    score_conn,
).sort_values("cust_id")

score_sql_ops = score_gr.get_executed_sqlops_by_method(exclude_date_filters=True)

print("do_labels" in score_sql_ops)
print("do_post_join_annotate" in score_sql_ops)
print(score_df.columns.tolist())

What changed in this run:

  • the frozen feature ops are replayed
  • date literals from the frozen training plan are rebound to the scoring graph's current cut_date
  • do_labels is omitted
  • label-dependent do_post_join_annotate and do_post_join_filters are omitted
  • date-node joins are skipped

This lets you keep feature logic fixed between training and scoring while still allowing the scoring graph to use its own current cutoff date.

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
The three runs are doing different things with the same graph structure:

  1. train=True dynamic run: generate SQL ops and execute them
  2. train=True frozen replay: reuse the exact executed SQL ops from step 1
  3. train=False frozen replay: reuse the frozen feature ops but omit labels and label-dependent post-join logic

The core API is:

plan = train_gr.freeze_execution_plan()

new_gr.apply_execution_plan(plan)
new_gr.do_transformations_sql()

Use get_executed_sqlops_by_method() or get_executed_op_records() if you want to inspect exactly what ran after execution.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: This walkthrough builds a two-table customer feature graph with the sample CSV files included in the repository. Run it from the repository root.

docs.title: What you will build
docs.text:
cust.csv                       orders.csv
one row per customer           many rows per customer
        id  1 ───────────── *  customer_id
           output grain          reduce before join

The graph uses order history to create customer features and uses future order rows to create a customer label.

docs.title: 1. Install the project
docs.text:
pip install -e ".[dev]"

The sample files live under tests/data/cust_data/.

docs.title: 2. Define the nodes
docs.text:
import datetime as dt
from pathlib import Path

from graphreduce.enum import ComputeLayerEnum, PeriodUnit
from graphreduce.graph_reduce import GraphReduce
from graphreduce.node import DynamicNode

data_dir = Path("tests/data/cust_data")

customers = DynamicNode(
    fpath=str(data_dir / "cust.csv"),
    fmt="csv",
    pk="id",
    prefix="cust",
    compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.pandas,
)

orders = DynamicNode(
    fpath=str(data_dir / "orders.csv"),
    fmt="csv",
    pk="id",
    prefix="ord",
    date_key="ts",
    compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.pandas,
)

The prefixes are unique, so output columns retain their source: cust_name comes from customers and ord_amount_sum comes from orders. The orders node has a date_key; the static customer table does not need one.

docs.title: 3. Configure the graph
docs.text:
graph = GraphReduce(
    name="customer_quickstart",
    parent_node=customers,
    compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.pandas,
    cut_date=dt.datetime(2023, 6, 30),
    compute_period_val=365,
    compute_period_unit=PeriodUnit.day,
    auto_features=True,
    label_node=orders,
    label_field="id",
    label_operation="count",
    label_period_val=30,
    label_period_unit=PeriodUnit.day,
)

This declares:

  • one output row per customer;
  • a one-year order-history window ending just before June 30, 2023; and
  • a 30-day future window beginning just after that cutoff for the order-count label.

docs.title: 4. Connect the nodes
docs.text:
graph.add_node(customers)
graph.add_node(orders)

graph.add_entity_edge(
    parent_node=customers,
    relation_node=orders,
    parent_key="id",
    relation_key="customer_id",
    reduce=True,
)

reduce=True is essential here. It tells GraphReduce to aggregate all matching orders to one row per customer_id before joining them to customers.

docs.title: 5. Execute and inspect
docs.text:
graph.do_transformations()

features = graph.parent_node.df
print(features.shape)
print(features.head())

The sample produces four rows—one for each customer. The exact feature count may evolve as automatic feature generation improves, so assert the intended row grain and required columns rather than a fixed total column count.

assert len(features) == 4
assert features["cust_id"].is_unique
assert "ord_id_label" in features.columns

Customers with no order in the label window have a null label after the left join. If “no matching event” means zero for your task, fill that value explicitly before model training; do not apply that rule blindly to targets where missing has a different meaning.

docs.title: What happened
docs.text:
GraphReduce performed the following work:

  1. Loaded and prefixed both CSV files.
  2. Filtered order feature rows to the configured historical window.
  3. Generated order aggregates grouped by ord_customer_id.
  4. Left-joined those aggregates to customers.
  5. Counted orders in the future label window and joined the label.
  6. Stored the customer-grain result on graph.parent_node.df.

docs.title: Post-Join Dependencies
docs.text: Some annotations and filters require columns from one or more child nodes. A post-join dependency prevents that operation from running until those children have been merged.

docs.title: Dataframe nodes
docs.text:
Use method_requires with node classes:

from graphreduce.context import method_requires
from graphreduce.node import GraphReduceNode


class OrderNode(GraphReduceNode):
    # Implement the required node methods here.
    ...


class CustomerNode(GraphReduceNode):
    @method_requires(nodes=[OrderNode])
    def do_post_join_annotate(self):
        signup = self.colabbr("signup_date")
        self.df[self.colabbr("days_to_last_order")] = (
            self.df["ord_ts_max"] - self.df[signup]
        ).dt.days

    # Implement the other required node methods here.
    ...

GraphReduce records merged relation classes on the parent. The decorated method returns without executing until every required class is present.

For multiple dependencies:

@method_requires(nodes=[OrderNode, NotificationNode])
def do_post_join_filters(self):
    self.df = self.df[
        self.df["ord_id_count"].notna()
        | self.df["not_id_count"].notna()
    ]

docs.title: SQL nodes
docs.text:
SQL nodes accept dependency instances as constructor settings:

customers = SQLNode(
    # ...normal node configuration...
    do_post_join_annotate_ops=[...],
    do_post_join_annotate_requires=[orders],
    do_post_join_filters_ops=[...],
    do_post_join_filters_requires=[orders, notifications],
)

The SQL path checks whether columns with each required node's prefix are available before returning the configured operations.

docs.title: Guidance
docs.text:
• Use pre-join hooks for logic that depends only on the node's own columns.
  • Use post-join hooks only when another relation is genuinely required.
  • Depend on the smallest set of nodes needed by the expression.
  • Reference prefixed columns, because source names have already changed by the time a post-join method runs.
  • Cover dependency order with a small graph test; the operation's correctness depends on both graph topology and prefixes.

docs.title: SQL Backends and Dynamic Queries
docs.text:
SQL nodes express graph operations as composable SQL and execute them through a backend client. Start with a single node to verify source loading, prefixes, and generated SQL before building a multi-table graph.

ComputeLayerEnum includes SQL dialects for:

  • SQLite
  • DuckDB
  • Snowflake
  • Databricks SQL
  • AWS Athena
  • AWS Redshift
  • PostgreSQL
  • MySQL
  • Trino

Client setup and backend-specific behavior vary. Choose the matching enum and node subclass; there is no generic ComputeLayerEnum.sql.

docs.title: DuckDB single-node example
docs.text:
This mirrors the test_duckdb_node pattern and shows the exact dynamic query construction call:

from pathlib import Path
import duckdb

from graphreduce.node import DuckdbNode
from graphreduce.enum import ComputeLayerEnum

data_path = Path("tests/data/cust_data")
con = duckdb.connect()

node = DuckdbNode(
    fpath=f"'{data_path / 'cust.csv'}'",
    pk="id",
    prefix="cust",
    compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.duckdb,
    client=con,
    columns=["id", "name"],
    table_name="customer",  # required for filesystem-backed DuckDB reads
)

print(node.build_query(node.do_data()))
print(node.build_query(node.do_annotate()))

What this demonstrates:

  • node.do_data() emits the base SQL op sequence
  • node.build_query(...) compiles SQL text from those ops
  • node.do_annotate() shows prefixed column-selection SQL generation

docs.title: SQLite custom-node example
docs.text:
This version shows dynamic SQL from user-defined node methods.

import sqlite3
from pathlib import Path
import typing
import pandas as pd

from graphreduce.node import SQLNode
from graphreduce.enum import ComputeLayerEnum, SQLOpType
from graphreduce.models import sqlop

data_path = Path("tests/data/cust_data")
conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")

# Load the CSV into a SQLite table.
pd.read_csv(data_path / "orders.csv").to_sql("orders", conn, index=False, if_exists="replace")

class OrdersSQLNode(SQLNode):
    def do_filters(self) -> typing.List[sqlop]:
        return [sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.where, opval=f"{self.colabbr('ts')} >= '2023-01-01'")]

    def do_reduce(self, reduce_key):
        return [
            sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.aggfunc, opval=f"count(*) as {self.colabbr('num_orders')}"),
            sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.agg, opval=f"{self.colabbr(reduce_key)}"),
        ]

orders = OrdersSQLNode(
    fpath="orders",
    prefix="ord",
    pk="id",
    date_key="ts",
    client=conn,
    compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.sqlite,
    columns=["id", "customer_id", "ts", "amount"],
)

print(orders.build_query(orders.do_data()))
print(orders.build_query(orders.do_annotate()))
print(orders.build_query(orders.do_filters()))
print(orders.build_query(orders.do_filters() + orders.do_reduce("customer_id")))

conn.close()

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
• You define SQL behavior in small composable ops.
  • GraphReduce compiles those ops into executable SQL at runtime.
  • The same node/graph abstraction can target different SQL engines by changing backend configuration and node class.

docs.title: SQL Operations and Dialects
docs.text: GraphReduce represents SQL as small sqlop objects. A SQLNode combines those objects with its current source reference, and build_query() renders an executable statement for the selected compute layer.

docs.title: Operation types
docs.text:
Common SQLOpType values include:

Type SQL role select Projection or derived column where Filter predicate aggfunc Aggregate expression in the projection agg GROUP BY expression having Post-aggregation filter order Sort expression window Window expression

docs.title: Build a query
docs.text:
import sqlite3

from graphreduce.enum import ComputeLayerEnum, SQLOpType
from graphreduce.models import sqlop
from graphreduce.node import SQLNode

connection = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")

orders = SQLNode(
    fpath="orders",
    prefix="ord",
    pk="id",
    date_key="ts",
    compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.sqlite,
    client=connection,
    columns=["id", "customer_id", "ts", "amount"],
)

ops = [
    sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.where, opval="ord_ts >= '2023-01-01'"),
    sqlop(
        optype=SQLOpType.aggfunc,
        opval="sum(ord_amount) as ord_amount_sum",
    ),
    sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.agg, opval="ord_customer_id"),
]

print(orders.build_query(ops))

The node knows its source relation and prefixes. The operations specify only the changes needed for this stage.

docs.title: Put operations on a node
docs.text:
For reusable behavior, subclass SQLNode:

class OrderNode(SQLNode):
    def do_filters(self):
        return [
            sqlop(
                optype=SQLOpType.where,
                opval=f"{self.colabbr('amount')} >= 0",
            )
        ]

    def do_reduce(self, reduce_key):
        return [
            sqlop(
                optype=SQLOpType.aggfunc,
                opval=(
                    f"sum({self.colabbr('amount')}) "
                    f"as {self.colabbr('amount_sum')}"
                ),
            ),
            sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.agg, opval=self.key_sql(reduce_key)),
        ]

do_transformations_sql() calls these methods while traversing the graph, compiles the returned operations, and creates intermediate references.

docs.title: Dialect selection matters
docs.text:
Choose the enum value for the actual engine—such as sqlite, duckdb, snowflake, redshift, athena, postgres, mysql, trino, or databricks. GraphReduce uses it for date arithmetic, quoting, temporary objects, and other syntax differences.

Portable custom SQL should use simple expressions and GraphReduce helpers such as colabbr() and key_sql(). Backend-specific functions may still require a specialized node implementation.

  • SQL backends and dynamic query construction

docs.title: Choose a Compute Layer
docs.text:
GraphReduce keeps the graph structure and node operations from the execution engine. Switching engines is easiest when the graph uses DynamicNode and automatic features; custom node methods remain backend-specific.

The graph topology, time-window configuration, and intended output grain form the portable contract. Engine-specific expressions, clients, storage access, and materialization behavior remain integration concerns.

docs.title: Dataframe nodes
docs.text:
The same basic node configuration works across dataframe engines:

from graphreduce.enum import ComputeLayerEnum
from graphreduce.node import DynamicNode

customers = DynamicNode(
    fpath="customers.parquet",
    fmt="parquet",
    pk="id",
    prefix="cust",
    compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.pandas,  # or dask, spark, or daft
)

Set the graph to the same compute layer:

graph = GraphReduce(
    parent_node=customers,
    compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.pandas,
    auto_features=True,
)

Spark also needs spark_sqlctx where required by the current API. Storage paths must be readable by the chosen engine; a local path that works in pandas may not be visible to a distributed Spark job.

docs.title: SQL nodes
docs.text:
SQL execution uses SQLNode or a backend-specific subclass and the SQL entry point:

import duckdb

from graphreduce.enum import ComputeLayerEnum
from graphreduce.node import DuckdbNode

connection = duckdb.connect()

customers = DuckdbNode(
    fpath="customers",
    table_name="customers",
    fmt="sql",
    pk="id",
    prefix="cust",
    compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.duckdb,
    client=connection,
    columns=["id", "name"],
)

graph = GraphReduce(
    parent_node=customers,
    compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.duckdb,
    sql_client=connection,
)
graph.add_node(customers)
graph.do_transformations_sql()

Client construction, credentials, catalogs, and temporary-object behavior vary by backend. Use the matching end-to-end example before porting a large graph.

docs.title: What is portable
docs.text:
Usually portable:

  • graph topology and edge keys;
  • parent-grain and time-window configuration;
  • DynamicNode automatic feature intent; and
  • basic aggregate semantics.

Usually backend-specific:

  • custom dataframe expressions;
  • custom SQL strings and functions;
  • type coercion and timestamp syntax;
  • identifier quoting;
  • connection and catalog setup; and
  • materialization/checkpoint behavior.

See Same graph, multiple backends for side-by-side implementations.

docs.title: Verify Point-in-Time Correctness
docs.text: Time leakage occurs when a feature uses information that would not have been available at prediction time. GraphReduce prevents this by applying separate historical and future windows around a cutoff.

docs.title: Window contract
docs.text:
For cutoff T:

features: T - compute period < timestamp < T
labels:   T                  < timestamp < T + label period

For non-null timestamps, the comparisons are strict. Rows on any boundary are excluded.

docs.title: Inspect one node
docs.text:
Run this example from the repository root:

import datetime as dt
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd

from graphreduce.enum import ComputeLayerEnum, PeriodUnit
from graphreduce.node import DynamicNode

orders = DynamicNode(
    fpath=str(Path("tests/data/cust_data/orders.csv")),
    fmt="csv",
    pk="id",
    prefix="ord",
    date_key="ts",
    compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.pandas,
    cut_date=dt.datetime(2023, 7, 1),
    compute_period_val=365,
    compute_period_unit=PeriodUnit.day,
    label_period_val=60,
    label_period_unit=PeriodUnit.day,
)

orders.do_data()

feature_rows = orders.prep_for_features()
label_rows = orders.prep_for_labels()

print(feature_rows[["ord_id", "ord_ts"]])
print(label_rows[["ord_id", "ord_ts"]])

feature_times = pd.to_datetime(feature_rows["ord_ts"])
label_times = pd.to_datetime(label_rows["ord_ts"])
cutoff = pd.Timestamp("2023-07-01")

assert (feature_times < cutoff).all()
assert (label_times > cutoff).all()

do_data() loads the CSV and adds the ord_ prefix. The two helper methods return filtered frames; they do not mix feature and label rows. The explicit pd.to_datetime() calls above normalize the result before the verification assertions.

docs.text:
Set shared time controls on GraphReduce:

graph = GraphReduce(
    parent_node=customers,
    compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.pandas,
    cut_date=dt.datetime(2023, 7, 1),
    compute_period_val=365,
    compute_period_unit=PeriodUnit.day,
    label_node=orders,
    label_field="id",
    label_operation="count",
    label_period_val=60,
    label_period_unit=PeriodUnit.day,
    auto_features=True,
)

During graph hydration, these values are pushed to the nodes so one execution uses a consistent reference time.

docs.title: Checklist before training
docs.text:
• Give every time-varying node the correct date_key.
  • Confirm timestamps represent availability time, not merely when an event was later recorded or updated.
  • Treat static dimensions without a date_key carefully if their attributes can change over time.
  • Decide whether rows with null timestamps should be retained. The dataframe feature helper currently retains them, while SQL comparisons normally do not.
  • Test both helper windows on a small known sample.
  • Assert the output grain after all joins.
  • Reserve validation and test cutoffs that are later than training cutoffs.

GraphReduce can enforce configured timestamps; it cannot infer whether a source column itself contains future-derived information. Declare or remove such columns before feature generation. See Feature schema profiles for explicit unsafe-column handling.

#!/usr/bin/env python
"""Custom duckdb GraphReduce example using all cust_data nodes."""

from __future__ import annotations

import datetime

try:
    import duckdb
except Exception as exc:  # pragma: no cover
    print(f"duckdb not available: {exc}", flush=True)
    raise SystemExit(0)

from graphreduce.enum import ComputeLayerEnum, SQLOpType
from graphreduce.graph_reduce import GraphReduce
from graphreduce.models import sqlop
from graphreduce.node import SQLNode


class CustNode(SQLNode):
    def do_annotate(self):
        return [
            sqlop(
                optype=SQLOpType.select,
                opval=f"*, length(coalesce({self.colabbr('name')}, '')) as {self.colabbr('name_length')}",
            )
        ]

    def do_filters(self):
        return [sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.where, opval=f"{self.colabbr('id')} is not null")]

    def do_normalize(self):
        return [
            sqlop(
                optype=SQLOpType.select,
                opval=f"*, lower(trim(coalesce({self.colabbr('name')}, ''))) as {self.colabbr('name')}",
            )
        ]

    def do_reduce(self, reduce_key):
        return None

    def do_post_join_annotate(self):
        return [
            sqlop(
                optype=SQLOpType.select,
                opval="*"
                + ", coalesce(ord_num_orders, 0) + coalesce(not_num_notifications, 0) + coalesce(not_num_engaged_interactions, 0) as cust_total_events"
                + ", case"
                + " when (coalesce(ord_num_orders, 0) + coalesce(not_num_notifications, 0) + coalesce(not_num_engaged_interactions, 0)) >= 5 then 'high'"
                + " when (coalesce(ord_num_orders, 0) + coalesce(not_num_notifications, 0) + coalesce(not_num_engaged_interactions, 0)) >= 2 then 'medium'"
                + " else 'low' end as cust_activity_tier",
            )
        ]

    def do_post_join_filters(self):
        return [sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.where, opval="cust_total_events >= 0")]


class OrderNode(SQLNode):
    def do_annotate(self):
        return [
            sqlop(
                optype=SQLOpType.select,
                opval=f"*, cast({self.colabbr('amount')} as double) as {self.colabbr('amount_dbl')}",
            )
        ]

    def do_filters(self):
        return [sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.where, opval=f"{self.colabbr('ts')} >= '2022-01-01'")]

    def do_normalize(self):
        return [
            sqlop(
                optype=SQLOpType.select,
                opval=f"*, coalesce({self.colabbr('amount_dbl')}, 0.0) as {self.colabbr('amount_dbl')}",
            )
        ]

    def do_reduce(self, reduce_key):
        return [
            sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.aggfunc, opval=f"count(distinct {self.colabbr(self.pk)}) as {self.colabbr('num_orders')}"),
            sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.aggfunc, opval=f"sum({self.colabbr('amount_dbl')}) as {self.colabbr('sum_amount')}"),
            sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.aggfunc, opval=f"avg({self.colabbr('amount_dbl')}) as {self.colabbr('avg_amount')}"),
            sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.agg, opval=f"{self.colabbr(reduce_key)}"),
        ]


class OrderProductsNode(SQLNode):
    def do_annotate(self):
        return [
            sqlop(
                optype=SQLOpType.select,
                opval=f"*, cast({self.colabbr('product_id')} as int) as {self.colabbr('product_id_int')}",
            )
        ]

    def do_filters(self):
        return [sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.where, opval=f"{self.colabbr('product_id_int')} is not null")]

    def do_normalize(self):
        return None

    def do_reduce(self, reduce_key):
        return [
            sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.aggfunc, opval=f"count({self.colabbr(self.pk)}) as {self.colabbr('num_order_products')}"),
            sqlop(
                optype=SQLOpType.aggfunc,
                opval=f"count(distinct {self.colabbr('product_id_int')}) as {self.colabbr('num_distinct_products')}",
            ),
            sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.agg, opval=f"{self.colabbr(reduce_key)}"),
        ]


class NotificationNode(SQLNode):
    def do_annotate(self):
        return [
            sqlop(
                optype=SQLOpType.select,
                opval=f"*, strftime({self.colabbr('ts')}, '%m') as {self.colabbr('ts_month')}",
            )
        ]

    def do_filters(self):
        return [sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.where, opval=f"{self.colabbr('ts')} >= '2022-01-01'")]

    def do_normalize(self):
        return None

    def do_reduce(self, reduce_key):
        return [
            sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.aggfunc, opval=f"count(distinct {self.colabbr(self.pk)}) as {self.colabbr('num_notifications')}"),
            sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.aggfunc, opval=f"max({self.colabbr('ts')}) as {self.colabbr('max_notification_ts')}"),
            sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.aggfunc, opval=f"sum(coalesce(ni_num_interactions, 0)) as {self.colabbr('num_interactions')}"),
            sqlop(
                optype=SQLOpType.aggfunc,
                opval=f"sum(coalesce(ni_num_engaged_interactions, 0)) as {self.colabbr('num_engaged_interactions')}",
            ),
            sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.agg, opval=f"{self.colabbr(reduce_key)}"),
        ]


class NotificationInteractionsNode(SQLNode):
    def do_annotate(self):
        return [
            sqlop(
                optype=SQLOpType.select,
                opval=f"*, strftime({self.colabbr('ts')}, '%Y-%m-%d') as {self.colabbr('ts_day')}",
            )
        ]

    def do_filters(self):
        return [sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.where, opval=f"{self.colabbr('ts')} >= '2022-01-01'")]

    def do_normalize(self):
        return None

    def do_reduce(self, reduce_key):
        return [
            sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.aggfunc, opval=f"count({self.colabbr(self.pk)}) as {self.colabbr('num_interactions')}"),
            sqlop(
                optype=SQLOpType.aggfunc,
                opval=f"count(distinct {self.colabbr('interaction_type_id')}) as {self.colabbr('num_interaction_types')}",
            ),
            sqlop(
                optype=SQLOpType.aggfunc,
                opval=f"sum(coalesce(nit_is_engagement_type, 0)) as {self.colabbr('num_engaged_interactions')}",
            ),
            sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.agg, opval=f"{self.colabbr(reduce_key)}"),
        ]


class NotificationInteractionTypeNode(SQLNode):
    def do_annotate(self):
        return [
            sqlop(
                optype=SQLOpType.select,
                opval="*"
                + f", lower(trim({self.colabbr('name')})) as {self.colabbr('name')}"
                + f", case when lower(trim({self.colabbr('name')})) in ('clicked', 'dismissed') then 1 else 0 end as {self.colabbr('is_engagement_type')}"
                + f", case when lower(trim({self.colabbr('name')})) like '%view%' then 1 else 0 end as {self.colabbr('is_view_event')}",
            )
        ]

    def do_filters(self):
        return [sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.where, opval=f"{self.colabbr('id')} is not null")]

    def do_normalize(self):
        return None

    def do_reduce(self, reduce_key):
        return [
            sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.aggfunc, opval=f"min({self.colabbr('name')}) as {self.colabbr('name')}"),
            sqlop(
                optype=SQLOpType.aggfunc,
                opval=f"max({self.colabbr('is_engagement_type')}) as {self.colabbr('is_engagement_type')}",
            ),
            sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.aggfunc, opval=f"max({self.colabbr('is_view_event')}) as {self.colabbr('is_view_event')}"),
            sqlop(optype=SQLOpType.agg, opval=f"{self.colabbr(reduce_key)}"),
        ]


def build_custom_duckdb_graph(con: duckdb.DuckDBPyConnection) -> GraphReduce:
    con.sql("CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW cust AS SELECT * FROM read_csv_auto('tests/data/cust_data/cust.csv', header=true)")

    cust = CustNode(fpath="cust", prefix="cust", pk="id", client=con, compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.duckdb, columns=["id", "name"])
    orders = OrderNode(
        fpath="orders",
        prefix="ord",
        pk="id",
        date_key="ts",
        client=con,
        compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.duckdb,
        columns=["id", "customer_id", "ts", "amount"],

    order_products = OrderProductsNode(

    gr = GraphReduce(

    return gr
