Usage:
  python examples/custom_pyspark_all_nodes.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import datetime
import os

try:
    from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
except Exception as exc:  # pragma: no cover
    print(f"pyspark not available: {exc}", flush=True)
    raise SystemExit(0)

from graphreduce.enum import ComputeLayerEnum
from graphreduce.graph_reduce import GraphReduce
from graphreduce.node import GraphReduceNode

DATA_PATH = "tests/data/cust_data"


def _safe_numeric(df, candidates: list[str]):
    for c in candidates:
        if c in df.columns:
            return F.coalesce(F.col(c).cast("double"), F.lit(0.0))
    return F.lit(0.0)


class CustNode(GraphReduceNode):
    def do_annotate(self):
        self.df = self.df.withColumn(
            self.colabbr("name_length"),
            F.length(F.coalesce(F.col(self.colabbr("name")), F.lit(""))),
        )
        return self.df

    def do_filters(self):
        self.df = self.df.filter(F.col(self.colabbr("id")).isNotNull())
        return self.df

    def do_normalize(self):
        self.df = self.df.withColumn(
            self.colabbr("name"),
            F.lower(F.trim(F.coalesce(F.col(self.colabbr("name")), F.lit("")))),
        )
        return self.df

    def do_reduce(self, reduce_key):
        return self.df

    def do_labels(self, reduce_key):
        return self.df

    def do_post_join_annotate(self):
        ord_ct = F.coalesce(F.col("ord_num_orders"), F.lit(0))
        not_ct = F.coalesce(F.col("not_num_notifications"), F.lit(0))
        engaged = F.coalesce(F.col("not_num_engaged_interactions"), F.lit(0))

        self.df = self.df.withColumn("cust_total_events", ord_ct + not_ct + engaged).withColumn(
            "cust_activity_tier",
            F.when(F.col("cust_total_events") >= 5, F.lit("high"))
            .when(F.col("cust_total_events") >= 2, F.lit("medium"))
            .otherwise(F.lit("low")),
        )
        return self.df

    def do_post_join_filters(self):
        self.df = self.df.filter(F.col("cust_total_events") >= 0)
        return self.df


class OrderNode(GraphReduceNode):
    def do_annotate(self):
        self.df = self.df.withColumn(self.colabbr("amount_dbl"), F.col(self.colabbr("amount")).cast("double"))
        return self.df

    def do_filters(self):
        self.df = self.df.filter(F.col(self.colabbr("ts")) >= F.lit("2022-01-01"))
        return self.df

    def do_normalize(self):
        self.df = self.df.withColumn(self.colabbr("amount_dbl"), F.coalesce(F.col(self.colabbr("amount_dbl")), F.lit(0.0)))
        return self.df

    def do_reduce(self, reduce_key):
        return (
            self.prep_for_features()
            .groupBy(self.colabbr(reduce_key))
            .agg(
                F.countDistinct(F.col(self.colabbr(self.pk))).alias(self.colabbr("num_orders")),
                F.sum(F.col(self.colabbr("amount_dbl"))).alias(self.colabbr("sum_amount")),
                F.avg(F.col(self.colabbr("amount_dbl"))).alias(self.colabbr("avg_amount")),
            )
        )

    def do_labels(self, reduce_key):
        return self.df

    def do_post_join_annotate(self):
        return self.df

    def do_post_join_filters(self):
        return self.df


class OrderProductsNode(GraphReduceNode):
    def do_annotate(self):
        self.df = self.df.withColumn(
            self.colabbr("product_id_int"),
            F.col(self.colabbr("product_id")).cast("int"),
        )
        return self.df

    def do_filters(self):
        self.df = self.df.filter(F.col(self.colabbr("product_id_int")).isNotNull())
        return self.df

    def do_normalize(self):
        return self.df

    def do_reduce(self, reduce_key):
        return (
            self.prep_for_features()
            .groupBy(self.colabbr(reduce_key))
            .agg(
                F.count(F.col(self.colabbr(self.pk))).alias(self.colabbr("num_order_products")),
                F.countDistinct(F.col(self.colabbr("product_id_int"))).alias(self.colabbr("num_distinct_products")),
            )
        )

    def do_labels(self, reduce_key):
        return self.df

    def do_post_join_annotate(self):
        return self.df

    def do_post_join_filters(self):
        return self.df


class NotificationNode(GraphReduceNode):
    def do_annotate(self):
        self.df = self.df.withColumn(self.colabbr("ts_month"), F.date_format(F.col(self.colabbr("ts")), "MM"))
        return self.df

    def do_filters(self):
        self.df = self.df.filter(F.col(self.colabbr("ts")) >= F.lit("2022-01-01"))
        return self.df

    def do_normalize(self):
        return self.df

    def do_reduce(self, reduce_key):
        prepped = self.prep_for_features()
        ni_num_interactions = _safe_numeric(prepped, ["ni_num_interactions"])
        ni_num_engaged = _safe_numeric(prepped, ["ni_num_engaged_interactions"])
        return (
            prepped
            .groupBy(self.colabbr(reduce_key))
            .agg(
                F.countDistinct(F.col(self.colabbr(self.pk))).alias(self.colabbr("num_notifications")),
                F.max(F.col(self.colabbr("ts"))).alias(self.colabbr("max_notification_ts")),
                F.sum(ni_num_interactions).alias(self.colabbr("num_interactions")),
                F.sum(ni_num_engaged).alias(self.colabbr("num_engaged_interactions")),
            )
        )

    def do_labels(self, reduce_key):

    def do_post_join_annotate(self):
        return self.df

    def do_post_join_filters(self):
        return self.df


class NotificationInteractionsNode(GraphReduceNode):
    def do_annotate(self):
        self.df = self.df.withColumn(self.colabbr("ts_day"), F.date_format(F.col(self.colabbr("ts")), "yyyy-MM-dd"))
        return self.df

    def do_filters(self):
        self.df = self.df.filter(F.col(self.colabbr("ts")) >= F.lit("2022-01-01"))
        return self.df

    def do_normalize(self):
        return self.df

    def do_reduce(self, reduce_key):
        prepped = self.prep_for_features()
        engaged_expr = _safe_numeric(
            prepped,
            [
                "ni_nit_is_engagement_type",
                "nit_is_engagement_type",
                "ni_is_engagement_type",
            ],
        )
        return (
            prepped
            .groupBy(self.colabbr(reduce_key))
            .agg(
                F.count(F.col(self.colabbr(self.pk))).alias(self.colabbr("num_interactions")),
                F.countDistinct(F.col(self.colabbr("interaction_type_id"))).alias(self.colabbr("num_interaction_types")),
                F.sum(engaged_expr).alias(self.colabbr("num_engaged_interactions")),
            )
        )

    def do_labels(self, reduce_key):
        return self.df

    def do_post_join_annotate(self):
        return self.df

    def do_post_join_filters(self):
        return self.df


class NotificationInteractionTypeNode(GraphReduceNode):
    def do_annotate(self):
        self.df = self.df.withColumn(self.colabbr("name"), F.lower(F.trim(F.col(self.colabbr("name")))))
        return self.df

    def do_filters(self):
        self.df = self.df.filter(F.col(self.colabbr("id")).isNotNull())
        return self.df

    def do_normalize(self):
        return self.df

    def do_reduce(self, reduce_key):
        return (
            self.prep_for_features()
            .groupBy(self.colabbr(reduce_key))
            .agg(
                F.first(F.col(self.colabbr("name")), ignorenulls=True).alias(self.colabbr("name")),
                F.max(
                    F.when(F.col(self.colabbr("name")).isin("clicked", "dismissed"), F.lit(1)).otherwise(F.lit(0))
                ).alias(self.colabbr("is_engagement_type")),
                F.max(
                    F.when(F.col(self.colabbr("name")).contains("view"), F.lit(1)).otherwise(F.lit(0))
                ).alias(self.colabbr("is_view_event")),
            )
        )

    def do_labels(self, reduce_key):
        return self.df

    def do_post_join_annotate(self):
        return self.df

    def do_post_join_filters(self):
        return self.df


def build_custom_pyspark_graph(spark: SparkSession) -> GraphReduce:
    for table in [
        "cust",
        "orders",
        "order_products",
        "notifications",
        "notification_interactions",
        "notification_interaction_types",
    ]:
        spark.read.option("header", True).option("inferSchema", True).csv(
            os.path.join(DATA_PATH, f"{table}.csv")
        ).createOrReplaceTempView(table)

    cust = CustNode(
        fpath="cust",
        fmt="sql",
        prefix="cust",
        pk="id",
        compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.spark,
        columns=["id", "name"],
        spark_sqlctx=spark,
    )
    orders = OrderNode(
        fpath="orders",
        fmt="sql",
        prefix="ord",
        pk="id",
        date_key="ts",
        compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.spark,
        columns=["id", "customer_id", "ts", "amount"],
        spark_sqlctx=spark,
    )
    order_products = OrderProductsNode(
        fpath="order_products",
        fmt="sql",
        prefix="op",
        pk="id",
        compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.spark,
        columns=["id", "order_id", "product_id"],
        spark_sqlctx=spark,
    )
    notifications = NotificationNode(
        fpath="notifications",
        fmt="sql",
        prefix="not",
        pk="id",
        date_key="ts",
        compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.spark,
        columns=["id", "customer_id", "ts"],
        spark_sqlctx=spark,
    )
    notification_interactions = NotificationInteractionsNode(
        fpath="notification_interactions",
        fmt="sql",
        prefix="ni",
        pk="id",
        date_key="ts",
        compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.spark,
        columns=["id", "notification_id", "interaction_type_id", "ts"],
        spark_sqlctx=spark,
    )
    interaction_types = NotificationInteractionTypeNode(
        fpath="notification_interaction_types",
        fmt="sql",
        prefix="nit",
        pk="id",
        compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.spark,
        columns=["id", "name"],
        spark_sqlctx=spark,
    )

    gr = GraphReduce(
        name="custom_pyspark_all_nodes",
        parent_node=cust,
        compute_layer=ComputeLayerEnum.spark,
        spark_sqlctx=spark,
        cut_date=datetime.datetime(2023, 6, 30),
    )

    for node in [cust, orders, order_products, notifications, notification_interactions, interaction_types]:
        gr.add_node(node)

    gr.add_entity_edge(cust, orders, parent_key="id", relation_key="customer_id", reduce=True)
    gr.add_entity_edge(orders, order_products, parent_key="id", relation_key="order_id", reduce=True)
    gr.add_entity_edge(cust, notifications, parent_key="id", relation_key="customer_id", reduce=True)
    gr.add_entity_edge(notifications, notification_interactions, parent_key="id", relation_key="notification_id", reduce=True)
    gr.add_entity_edge(
        notification_interactions,
        interaction_types,
        parent_key="interaction_type_id",
        relation_key="id",
        reduce=True,
    )

    return gr


def run_custom_pyspark_all_nodes(spark: SparkSession | None = None):
    local_spark = spark or SparkSession.builder.appName("graphreduce-custom-all-nodes").getOrCreate()
    gr = build_custom_pyspark_graph(local_spark)
    gr.do_transformations()
    return gr.parent_node.df


def main() -> None:
    df = run_custom_pyspark_all_nodes()
    print("rows:", df.count(), flush=True)
    print("columns:", len(df.columns), flush=True)
    print("column_names:", df.columns, flush=True)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

This diagram is intentionally parallel to the Hello World visual, but this example is a custom data aggregation implementation: it uses GraphReduceNode subclasses, an explicit OrderNode.do_reduce(...), and a notifications edge with reduce=False to preserve child 1:n grain.

This example also highlights the pluggability of GraphReduce across multiple backends by showing the same graph semantics in both a pandas backend and a duckdb backend (SQLNode-based execution).

This example uses the same sample data as Hello World but sets reduce=False on the notifications.csv edge:

gr.add_entity_edge(cust_node, notifications_node, parent_key="id", relation_key="customer_id", reduce=False)

The key effect is that notifications are not rolled up to one row per customer before joining. That preserves the child 1:n grain at the parent join point and expands output rows beyond pure parent grain.

docs.title: When to use this pattern
docs.text: Use reduce=False when you want downstream logic to keep child-level records instead of collapsing them into aggregated features immediately.

docs.title: Fundamentals
docs.text:
GraphReduce treats relational feature engineering as graph execution. The graph makes three decisions explicit:

  1. What does one output row represent? The parent_node defines this grain.
  2. How are tables related? Each edge records the key pair and whether the relation must be reduced.
  3. Which rows are valid at prediction time? Date keys and graph-level windows separate historical features from future labels.

docs.title: A small example
docs.text:
customers ──< orders ──< order_products
    │
    └───────< notifications

If customers is the parent node, a bottom-up execution works like this:

  1. Reduce order_products to one row per order.
  2. Join those features to orders.
  3. Reduce the enriched orders to one row per customer.
  4. Reduce notifications to one row per customer.
  5. Join both sets of customer-level features to customers.

This ordering preserves information from deep relations while keeping the final table at customer grain.

docs.title: The three objects
docs.text:
Object Represents Owns GraphReduceNode A table, file, or queryable relation Data access, filtering, annotation, normalization, reduction, labels Entity edge A parent/child relationship Join keys, reduce, and reduce_after_join behavior GraphReduce The full compute graph Parent grain, time windows, traversal, joins, and execution backend

DynamicNode supplies default behavior for automatic feature engineering. Subclass GraphReduceNode when a table needs custom logic. Use SQLNode or a backend-specific subclass when operations should be compiled into SQL.

docs.title: Four rules to remember
docs.text:
1. Every node needs a unique prefix.
  2. Every time-varying node needs a date_key for point-in-time filtering.
  3. Use reduce=True for a normal one-to-many child that must roll up to its parent.
  4. Read the result from graph.parent_node.df for dataframe execution; SQL execution instead maintains backend references and generated statements.

Continue with:

  • Operations pipeline
  • Joins and cardinality
  • Time windows and leakage safety
  • Core abstractions

docs.title: Joins and Cardinality
docs.text: The most important edge decision is whether a child relation should be reduced before it is joined. That decision determines the row grain of the result.

docs.title: Define an edge
docs.text:
graph.add_entity_edge(
    parent_node=customers,
    relation_node=orders,
    parent_key="id",
    relation_key="customer_id",
    reduce=True,
)

This means:

  • customers is on the one side of the relationship;
  • orders is on the many side;
  • customers.id = orders.customer_id is the join condition; and
  • orders must be aggregated by customer_id before the join.

GraphReduce uses a left join when it attaches the child result, so parent rows without matching child rows remain in the output.

docs.title: Choose the reduction mode
docs.text:
Configuration Behavior Typical use reduce=True Aggregate the child to its edge key, then join Preserve parent grain across a one-to-many relationship reduce=False Join the child rows directly Intentionally produce or preserve child grain reduce_after_join=True Join first, then reduce the enriched parent side Aggregate only after required child context is present

reduce and reduce_after_join cannot both be true.

docs.title: Why reduce=True is the normal choice
docs.text: If customer 7 has three orders, a raw join produces three customer rows. Reducing orders first produces one row containing summaries such as order count and total amount; joining that row back preserves one customer row.

docs.title: When reduce=False is appropriate
docs.text: Use it only when row multiplication is intended—for example, when building one output row per notification while attaching customer attributes. Verify the grain explicitly after execution. See Preserve child grain.

docs.title: Composite keys
docs.text:
Keys may be a string or an ordered list/tuple of strings:

graph.add_entity_edge(
    parent_node=accounts,
    relation_node=events,
    parent_key=("tenant_id", "account_id"),
    relation_key=("tenant_id", "account_id"),
    reduce=True,
)

Both sides must contain the same number of key columns, in matching order.

docs.title: Avoid accidental many-to-many joins
docs.text:
Before executing a graph, answer these questions for every edge:

  1. Is the parent key unique at the point of the join?
  2. How many child rows can match one parent row?
  3. Does the relation need to be reduced once, or after another child has joined?
  4. What should one row represent immediately after this edge?
  5. Can the row count be asserted on a small sample?

Prefixes prevent column-name collisions; they do not prevent row multiplication. Cardinality must be modeled deliberately.

docs.title: Operations Pipeline
docs.text: GraphReduce separates operations that use one table from operations that need joined data. This makes the location and timing of each transformation predictable.

docs.title: Node operations
docs.text:
Method When it runs Purpose do_data First Load a dataframe or establish a SQL source do_annotate Before reduction Add columns derived from the node alone do_filters Before reduction Remove rows using node-local conditions do_normalize Before reduction Clean or normalize node-local values do_reduce During edge traversal Aggregate a relation to its parent key do_labels During edge traversal Aggregate target values from the label window do_post_join_annotate After a child join Add columns that depend on joined data do_post_join_filters After a child join Filter using joined data do_post_join_reduce After a child join, when configured Reduce an enriched intermediate relation

DynamicNode implements the required hooks with automatic/default behavior. A custom GraphReduceNode subclass must implement the abstract hooks, even when a hook only contains pass.

docs.title: Dataframe execution
docs.text:
GraphReduce.do_transformations() performs this high-level sequence:

hydrate graph configuration
        │
load every node
        │
check prefix uniqueness
        │
annotate → filter → normalize each node
        │
traverse edges from leaves toward the parent
        │
for each edge:
  reduce child if requested
  + generate automatic features if enabled
  + join child result to parent
  + compute/join labels when applicable
  + run eligible post-join operations
        │
materialized parent dataframe

The traversal is bottom-up. Features created on a deep child can therefore be carried through an intermediate node and reduced again at the next edge.

docs.title: SQL execution
docs.text:
GraphReduce.do_transformations_sql() follows the same relational intent, but node methods return lists of sqlop values. GraphReduce compiles those values, creates intermediate references in the SQL backend, and records generated SQL in graph.sql_ops.

SQL execution is not a drop-in call on a dataframe graph. Use SQLNode or a backend-specific SQL subclass, supply the appropriate client, and select the matching ComputeLayerEnum value.

  • Custom node operations

docs.title: Time Windows and Leakage Safety
docs.text:
GraphReduce divides dated rows around a cutoff T:

feature window                         label window
(T - compute period, T)                (T, T + label period)
──────────────────────●────────────────●──────────────────
          past                         T          future

For non-null timestamps, the base implementation uses strict comparisons. A row exactly at T, at the history start, or at the label-window end is excluded.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Setting Meaning cut_date Point in time at which features are evaluated compute_period_val + compute_period_unit How far backward feature rows may extend label_period_val + label_period_unit How far forward label rows may extend Node date_key Timestamp column used to filter that node

Graph-level values are pushed into nodes during graph hydration, keeping the cutoff and windows consistent across the graph.

docs.title: Exact base-class contract
docs.text:
For a dated node, prep_for_features() applies:

cut_date - compute_period < date_key < cut_date

prep_for_labels() applies:

cut_date < date_key < cut_date + label_period

Undated nodes are not filtered by these helpers. Set date_key on every node whose rows become available over time.

The dataframe feature path currently retains rows whose configured date_key is null, while SQL WHERE comparisons normally exclude them. Labels exclude null timestamps. Decide whether unknown timestamps are valid for your problem, and filter them explicitly when you need identical behavior across backends.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
With a cutoff of 2024-01-01, a 365-day compute period, and a 30-day label period:

  • features can use rows after 2023-01-01 and before 2024-01-01;
  • labels can use rows after 2024-01-01 and before 2024-01-31; and
  • a row stamped exactly 2024-01-01 belongs to neither window.

docs.title: Leakage checklist
docs.text:
• Use the timestamp that represents availability, not merely when a source event happened.
  • Declare a date_key for every time-varying node.
  • Confirm timezone and timestamp precision before comparing boundaries.
  • Define and test a policy for null timestamps.
  • Keep label-derived and future-derived fields out of the feature graph.
  • Fit schema profiles and category selections using training data only.
  • Inspect the minimum and maximum timestamps in a small materialized result.
  • Build multiple cutoffs for backtesting instead of making a random row split across one temporal snapshot.

GraphReduce can enforce configured time boundaries, but it cannot infer when a business value truly became knowable. That remains part of the dataset's semantic contract.

See Point-in-time tutorial for an executable check.
